items.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023
items.q: I remember going to see Dizzy down at Henry Street Settlement in New York and he had a band... I loved what Bird was playing but I couldn’t understand it. I would sit there and go whoa — like listening to — all right Bird and Dizzy Gillespie.

ctx.x: And down at Number 22 was “The Hustle.”

Oh yeah. I grew up listening to all that music. Well hearing it. I was hearing it in the background ‘cause I had family members that really loved that stuff. But at that time, in 1975, I was at the time, I started out at the High School of Music & Art. I was a freshman at that time, and I was discovering Charlie Parker and Dizzy and Freddie Hubbard. That’s what I was getting into. I was also really into classical music so I was discovering some © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

wonderful recordings like there’s a recording of the Philadelphia, New York, and I want to say Chicago Symphony brass sections playing the Gabrieli Canzon. It was a very famous recording that was put out by I want to say RCA. And I had a really good trumpet teacher in high school named Sidney Baker who was from that tradition. So you just, when you’re around it that’s what you know. And mind you, this is before the Internet. So if you wanted to really seek out information you had to really put some — you had to…

items.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023
items.q: And then I remembered going to see Dizzy down at Henry Street Settlement in New York and he had a band that was kind of playing funky at the time

ctx.x: When did the idea, I mean you’re playing a single note instrument. Do you remember around what age you were when you started to be curious and understand about how single notes match up with chord symbols, and how chord symbols work?

Okay so my thing is this. And I share this openly with my students and I let them know, don’t be scared. I am the poster child for dyslexia. So the whole idea of the note and how it matches up to a chord, that was a nightmare for me. I knew what the note sounded like, and I could hear the chords, but making the match of the mathematics was a very major challenge for me. So I could play on “Rhythm” changes, I could play “Rhythm” changes, I could do standards, because I had really good ears, before I figured out…

Baroque and Renaissance music. So I remember sitting there and there was this woman dressed up all beautifully and she’s playing the harpsichord, and I say, in my ignorant South Bronx fashion, I go, “Hey man, that’s bebop.” Because I could hear [scats] and I went, “Oh man that’s bebop.” You know. Because listen, when I was in high school my girlfriend at the time, her father was a jazz guitar player, Doc Russell. And he took an interest in my development and they would have jam sessions at the house and I would…
